text: This is Phobos, the bigger of the two moons of Mars. It is small: about twenty-six kilometers long and eighteen across, roughly the size of a city. It is not round. It looks like a lumpy potato, dark as coal, and it is the closest moon to its planet anywhere in the solar system, only about six thousand kilometers above the surface of Mars. And it is falling. Slowly, but it is falling.

Stand on Phobos and look up, and Mars fills the sky. Not a dot, not a disk: a wall, more than eighty times wider than the full Moon looks from Earth. Phobos always keeps the same face toward it, the way our Moon does toward us. And gravity here is so weak that a good throw would send a baseball right off the moon.

Here is the strange part. Phobos goes around Mars once every seven hours and thirty-nine minutes. But a day on Mars is twenty-four hours and thirty-nine minutes long. So the moon laps the planet. From the ground on Mars, Phobos rises in the west, crosses the sky in about four hours, sets in the east, and comes back before the day is over. The other moon, Deimos, is farther out and takes thirty hours.

A moon that orbits faster than its planet turns is in trouble. Phobos raises a small tidal bulge on Mars, and because Mars spins slower than Phobos moves, that bulge trails behind the moon and tugs it backward. Every orbit, Phobos loses a little energy and drops a little lower: about one point eight centimeters a year. Deimos, outside the balance line, is slowly pushed the other way, the way our Moon drifts away from Earth.

Run the clock forward and the orbit tightens. The closer Phobos gets, the stronger the pull, and the faster it falls. Somewhere in the next twenty to seventy million years, depending on the study, Mars will pull harder on the near side of the moon than the moon can hold itself together. Then Phobos either breaks up into a ring around Mars, or the strongest chunks hit the planet. A two thousand fifteen model by Benjamin Black and Tushar Mittal favors the ring. An estimate from models, not a measurement.

This is a model of what that could look like. Phobos, probably loose and porous inside, stretches into a stream of rubble, and the rubble spreads along the old orbit into a thin, dark ring. Over millions of years it would rain back down onto the equator of Mars. Some researchers think this has happened before: that Mars has cycled between rings and moons several times, and Phobos is only the latest. That is a hypothesis, not settled history.

Look at the surface and you see a moon under stress. One end carries Stickney crater, about nine kilometers across, a hit that came close to breaking the moon apart. And all across Phobos run the grooves: long, straight, shallow trenches, typically a hundred to two hundred meters wide, tens of meters deep, some of them twenty kilometers long, in families of parallel lines.

Nobody is sure what made them. One idea: stretch marks. A two thousand sixteen study led by Terry Hurford found that most grooves line up with the stress Mars puts on the moon, which would mean the breakup has already begun. Another, from Kenneth Ramsley and James Head in two thousand eighteen: boulder tracks. When Stickney was blasted out, rocks rolled away across the surface, and in gravity this weak some rolled all the way around the moon. Each model explains many of the grooves; neither explains all of them alone.

text: Where did Phobos come from? It is dark and reddish like asteroids from the outer belt, so the easy answer was a captured asteroid. But a captured rock should be on a tilted, stretched orbit, and Phobos rides a near-perfect circle right over the equator of Mars. That is what you expect if a giant impact on Mars threw debris into orbit and the moons formed from it: a moon of Mars, made of Mars. Its low density and porous inside fit that story too.

Which is why a spacecraft is going to pick some up. Japan's space agency, JAXA, built the Martian Moons eXploration mission, MMX, with NASA, France and Germany. Launch on an H3 rocket from Tanegashima, scheduled for the morning of October twentieth, twenty twenty-six, Japan time. Reach Mars about a year later. Spend three years around Phobos. Drop a small French-German rover named Idefix onto the surface. Then land, scoop up at least ten grams of Phobos, and bring the capsule home in twenty thirty-one.

text: Ten grams does not sound like much. But a captured asteroid should hold more water and other volatiles than debris from a giant impact, which was heated on the way out, and the grains carry their ages. So that handful could settle where Phobos came from. And if it really is made partly of Mars, it would be the first piece of the planet ever brought back on purpose.

So here is Phobos today: a small, dark, cracked moon that laps its planet three times a day, slips a finger-width closer every year, and in a few tens of millions of years becomes a ring or a crater field. If the plan holds, in twenty thirty-one at least ten grams of it will be on a lab bench on Earth. The sources are on screen, and the estimates are labeled as estimates. Heartbeat Observatory.
